items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall the following special limit for sine:

Content:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = 1]

Content:
We can use this special limit to evaluate other limits, such as

Content:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin 2x}{x}.]

Content:
For this limit, notice that as [MATH: x\to0,] both the numerator and denominator approach [MATH: 0.] So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get
[MATH: %\lim_\limits{x \to 0} \: \dfrac{\sin 2x}{x} =
\dfrac00,]
which is an indeterminate form.

Content:
Instead, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:
[MATH: lim_(x → 0)(\sin 2x)/(x)|= lim_(x → 0)(2 ⋅ (\sin 2x)/(2x)); = 2 ⋅ lim_(x → 0)(\sin 2x)/(2x)]

Content:
Now, this limit looks very similar to our special limit for sine. So, if we make the substitution [MATH: \theta = 2x,] then, since [MATH: \theta \to 0] as [MATH: x \to 0,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 0} \: \dfrac{\sin {\color{blue}2x}}{\color{blue}2x}
= \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0} \: \dfrac{\sin {\color{blue}\theta}}{\color{blue}\theta}
= 1.]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: lim_(x → 0)(\sin 2x)/(x)|= 2 ⋅ lim_(x → 0)(\sin 2x)/(2x); = 2 ⋅ 1; = 2.]

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that as [MATH: x \to 5,] both numerator and denominator approach [MATH: 0.]

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get [MATH: \lim_{x \to5} \:\dfrac{\sin(x-5)}{15-3x} = \dfrac00,] which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit: [MATH: \lim_{\theta \to 0} \: \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\theta} = 1]

We rewrite the given limit using the algebra of limits, as follows: [MATH: lim_(x → 5)(\sin (x − 5))/(15 − 3x)|= lim_(x → 5)(\sin (x − 5))/((− 3)(x − 5)); = − (1)/(3) ⋅ lim_(x → 5)(\sin (x − 5))/(x − 5)]

Let [MATH: \theta =x-5.] Then, [MATH: \theta \to 0] as [MATH: x \to 5,] we have [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 5} \:\dfrac{\sin({\color{blue}x-5})}{\color{blue}x-5} = \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0} \:\dfrac{\sin{\color{blue}\theta}}{\color{blue}\theta} =1.]

Therefore, [MATH: − (1)/(3) ⋅ lim_(x → 5)(\sin (x − 5))/(x − 5)|= − (1)/(3) ⋅ 1; = − (1)/(3).]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we can simplify the limit using trigonometric identities, as follows:

[MATH: lim_(θ → 0)(\tan 2θ)/(θ)|= lim_(θ → 0)(((\sin 2θ)/(\cos 2θ)))/(θ); = lim_(θ → 0)((\sin 2θ)/(θ) ⋅ (1)/(\cos 2θ)); = lim_(θ → 0)(\sin 2θ)/(θ) ⋅ lim_(θ → 0)(1)/(\cos 2θ)]

Let's now evaluate the limits separately:

  • Consider the first limit. Notice that as [MATH: \theta \to 0,] both numerator and denominator approach [MATH: 0.]

    So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get [MATH: \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin 2\theta}{\theta} = \dfrac{0}{0},] which is an indeterminate form.

    Instead, let's recall the following special limit: [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin x}{x} =1]

    We rewrite the given limit using the algebra of limits, as follows: [MATH: lim_(θ → 0)(\sin 2θ)/(θ)|= lim_(θ → 0)(2 ⋅ (\sin 2θ)/(2θ)); = 2 ⋅ lim_(θ → 0)(\sin2θ)/(2θ)]

    Let [MATH: x = 2\theta.] Then, since [MATH: x\to0] as [MATH: \theta \to 0,] we have [MATH: 2 \cdot \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin \color{blue}2\theta}{\color{blue}2\theta} = 2 \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin \color{blue}x}{\color{blue}x} = 2 \cdot 1 =2.]

  • Consider the second limit. Evaluating it directly, we get [MATH: \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0} \: \dfrac{1}{ \cos 2\theta} = \dfrac{1}{ \cos 0} = \dfrac11 = 1.]

Therefore, we have

[MATH: lim_(θ → 0)(\sin 2θ)/(θ) ⋅ lim_(θ → 0)(1)/(\cos 2θ) = 2 ⋅ 1 = 2.]
